purpose: Verified literature candidates for editorial selection; this file is not the manuscript bibliography.

recommended_subset.reason: Direct early precedent for deep, convolutional, multilabel species-distribution modelling; useful in the Introduction if the manuscript explicitly distinguishes joint multilabel training from target-exclusive pretraining.

Direct empirical deep-SDM precedent showing that spatial environmental context and joint learning can improve predictions, especially for rare species; useful beside the manuscript's statement that shared representations may help data-limited targets.
Strong support for evaluating models across prediction tasks, biological levels and performance properties rather than treating one ranking or metric as general.
Direct presence-only benchmark showing that tuning and implementation choices materially affect model rankings and that default ensembles need not outperform single models.
Direct support for the manuscript's distinction between ordinary held-out accuracy and transferability to distinct locations or data sets.
Broad, authoritative transferability review supporting the manuscript's discussion of sampling bias, nonstationarity, environmental dissimilarity and other limits on geographic transfer.
Direct support for treating presence-background AUC as discrimination against the chosen background rather than occupancy accuracy, and for warning that extent affects AUC.
Direct support for the observation-process limitation: presence-only predictions can encode observer bias, and non-target-species inventory backgrounds do not by themselves remove it.
Direct community-science guidance supporting careful filtering, effort covariates and complete checklists; relevant to the bird observation-process caveat.

factual_corrections: Botella et al. (2018) is a Springer book chapter titled 'A Deep Learning Approach to Species Distribution Modelling', not a journal article.
Deneu et al. (2021) has six authors; Christophe Botella is the fourth author.
Harris (2015) is a single-author paper, and mistnet is a joint species distribution model rather than a pretraining method.
Chen, Xue and Gomes (2018) is an ICML/PMLR machine-learning paper, not an ecological SDM study, and the official PMLR record supplies no DOI.
Valavi et al.'s presence-only benchmark was first published online in 2021 but belongs to Ecological Monographs volume 92 issue 1 and is cited as 2022.
The blockCV paper was first published online in 2018 but belongs to Methods in Ecology and Evolution volume 10 issue 2 and is cited as 2019.
Jiménez-Valverde's DOI contains 2011, but the bibliographic issue year is 2012.
Kumar et al. (2022) is an ICLR conference paper with an official OpenReview URL but no DOI, volume or page range in the conference record.
The 2007 ensemble paper's authors are Miguel B. Araújo and Mark New.

csl.title: A Deep Learning Approach to Species Distribution Modelling
csl.container-title: Multimedia Tools and Applications for Environmental & Biodiversity Informatics

evidence.supported_claim: The chapter proposed a deep, convolutional, multilabel SDM and reported that spatial patterns in environmental variables improved prediction in its empirical study.
evidence.relevance: Useful as an early direct precedent for learning shared nonlinear representations across species.
evidence.limits: Its multilabel CNN jointly predicts species from environmental neighbourhoods; it does not test target-exclusive auxiliary pretraining, matched target-only networks or geographic transfer.
evidence.suggested_location: Introduction, after the first paragraph on shared representations, with an explicit distinction from the present pretraining design.

csl.title: Convolutional neural networks improve species distribution modelling by capturing the spatial structure of the environment

evidence.supported_claim: Using French plant occurrence data, joint-learning CNNs with environmental neighbourhoods outperformed ablated punctual alternatives; gains were especially apparent for species with few occurrences.
evidence.relevance: Direct empirical evidence that multi-species deep models can exploit shared environmental structure and sometimes help data-limited species.
evidence.limits: The comparison changes spatial input representation as well as model class, uses GBIF plant records in one domain, and does not isolate a pretrained-versus-target-only effect or test regional transfer.
evidence.suggested_location: Introduction as qualified precedent for deep multi-species SDMs; optionally Discussion when contrasting the present small inner gains with earlier within-domain results.

csl.title: Generating realistic assemblages with a joint species distribution model

evidence.supported_claim: Mistnet is a stochastic feedforward-neural-network JSDM that represents nonlinear environmental responses and non-independent co-occurrence attributed to unobserved heterogeneity; it improved held-out assemblage likelihood in a North American Breeding Bird Survey example.
evidence.relevance: Shows an earlier neural route for sharing information across species and modelling community-level dependence.
evidence.limits: Mistnet's estimand is a joint assemblage distribution and its advantage was assessed largely through assemblage likelihood, unlike the present target-specific AUC comparison and target-exclusive pretraining.
evidence.suggested_location: Only in a brief literature paragraph distinguishing joint community models from representation pretraining; omit if space is tight.

csl.title: End-to-End Learning for the Deep Multivariate Probit Model
csl.container-title: Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning

evidence.supported_claim: The deep multivariate probit model combines neural predictors with a multivariate probit correlation structure and improved joint likelihood on multi-entity tasks relative to tested competitors.
evidence.relevance: Provides general machine-learning context for deep models of correlated binary outcomes.
evidence.limits: This is not an ecological SDM evaluation, does not study presence-background observation processes, and optimizes joint multi-entity likelihood rather than testing transferable target-specific representations.
evidence.suggested_location: Usually omit; use only if the Introduction adds a compact taxonomy of deep multi-output models.

csl.title: A comprehensive evaluation of predictive performance of 33 species distribution models at species and community levels

evidence.supported_claim: Across 33 variants, five empirical community data sets and interpolation-to-extrapolation tasks, predictive performance depended strongly on model variant, data set and prediction task; rankings also changed with the performance property evaluated.
evidence.relevance: Supports the manuscript's use of multiple comparators and its separation of discrimination, calibration-like concerns, species-level prediction and transfer tasks.
evidence.limits: The study used presence-absence community data and many model variants; it does not benchmark the present presence-background design or establish the superiority of a specific comparator here.
evidence.suggested_location: Introduction when motivating credible conventional comparators, or Discussion where metric- and task-dependent rankings are emphasized.

csl.title: Predictive performance of presence-only species distribution models: a benchmark study with reproducible code

evidence.supported_claim: In a reproducible benchmark of presence-only methods evaluated with independent presence-absence data, tuning and fitting choices affected performance; a tuned ensemble ranked highest, while default biomod ensembles did no better than moderate single models.
evidence.relevance: Directly supports tuning credible conventional comparators and avoiding generic claims that an algorithm family or ensemble is intrinsically superior.
evidence.limits: The benchmark reanalysed 225 species from six regions under its own background and validation design; its rankings do not transfer automatically to the present taxa, predictors or geographic holdouts.
evidence.suggested_location: Introduction or Methods around the tuned conventional benchmark; Discussion around the dependence of ensemble benefit on constituent fitting and implementation.

csl.title: Outstanding Challenges in the Transferability of Ecological Models

evidence.supported_claim: This expert synthesis identifies species traits, sampling bias, biotic interactions, nonstationarity and environmental dissimilarity as determinants of transferred predictions, and highlights the lack of broadly applicable transferability metrics.
evidence.relevance: Provides direct conceptual support for treating regional transfer as a distinct inferential task and for qualifying what a held-region result can establish.
evidence.limits: It is a broad review and priority-setting exercise, not a quantitative estimate of any transfer penalty or a validation of the present design.
evidence.suggested_location: Introduction after defining intended transfer; Discussion in the paragraph on composition, support and nonstationarity.

csl.title: Assessing transferability of ecological models: an underappreciated aspect of statistical validation

evidence.supported_claim: Conventional validation need not assess generality to distinct locations, times or data sets; the authors recommend non-random grouping across those dimensions and show in a trout case study that high in-sample machine-learning performance can coexist with poor transfer.
evidence.relevance: Directly supports the manuscript's separation of inner development performance from held-region and mainland-to-Tasmania transfer.
evidence.limits: The empirical illustration involved two stream fishes and specific algorithms; it does not imply that flexible models always transfer poorly or quantify the present effect.
evidence.suggested_location: Introduction beside the sentence that gains should persist under the intended form of transfer.

csl.title: blockCV: An R package for generating spatially or environmentally separated folds for k-fold cross-validation of species distribution models

evidence.supported_claim: Random cross-validation can underestimate prediction error for structured data; blockCV implements spatially or environmentally separated folds and tools for exploring candidate block structure.
evidence.relevance: Supports the methodological rationale for complete projected spatial blocks in bird inner folds.
evidence.limits: It is principally a software/method paper. Citing it does not show that this manuscript's 50-km blocks eliminate dependence or reproduce the outer transfer task; Roberts et al. (2017) already covers the broader principle.
evidence.suggested_location: Methods beside the bird spatial-fold description only if a software/method-specific citation is wanted; otherwise the existing Roberts citation is adequate.

csl.title: Predicting into unknown space? Estimating the area of applicability of spatial prediction models

evidence.supported_claim: The authors define a predictor-space dissimilarity index and area of applicability; in their simulations, cross-validation error was comparable within the estimated area but did not apply outside it.
evidence.relevance: Useful for explaining that geographic holdouts can contain predictor combinations inadequately represented in training and that this should be diagnosed explicitly.
evidence.limits: The present manuscript has not reported an area-of-applicability analysis, so the paper cannot support a claim that environmental extrapolation caused the observed regional results.
evidence.suggested_location: Discussion as a future diagnostic or limitation, not as an explanation of the current outer result.

csl.title: Insights into the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) as a discrimination measure in species distribution modelling

evidence.supported_claim: AUC measures discrimination rather than calibration or ecological accuracy; with background rather than verified absences, its usual bounds and interpretation are altered, and its value depends on the evaluation domain.
evidence.relevance: Directly supports the manuscript's careful language that bird AUC estimates recorded-presence versus supported-background discrimination and that changing evaluation extent changes the task.
evidence.limits: The article argues strongly against AUC for potential-distribution evaluation. The present manuscript uses AUC for an explicitly narrower recording-discrimination estimand, so cite it to define that limitation rather than implying the reported comparisons are invalid.
evidence.suggested_location: Introduction after the Lobo et al. extent sentence or Discussion in the paragraph interpreting presence-background AUC.

csl.title: Model-Based Control of Observer Bias for the Analysis of Presence-Only Data in Ecology

evidence.supported_claim: Presence-only records can reflect spatial variation in observer activity; in a 62-plant evaluation, explicitly modelling known observer-bias covariates improved predictions and usually outperformed pseudoabsence or non-target-species inventory corrections.
evidence.relevance: Directly supports the manuscript's statement that donor-supported background indicates sampling support but does not separate ecological and recording processes.
evidence.limits: The paper's correction requires measured bias covariates and was evaluated in a plant case study. It does not show which process the present encoder learned or that the manuscript's X10 rule necessarily fails.
evidence.suggested_location: Introduction immediately after the paragraph on presence-background data and recording support; Discussion in the recording-richness interpretation paragraph.

csl.title: Analytical guidelines to increase the value of community science data: An example using eBird data to estimate species distributions

evidence.supported_claim: In eBird case studies, filtering observations, retaining complete checklists and modelling effort improved or did not harm model quality; degraded presence-only or incomplete-checklist data performed worse.
evidence.relevance: Supports explicit treatment of heterogeneous observation effort and the manuscript's refusal to interpret community-science recording discrimination as occupancy.
evidence.limits: The guidance is based on semi-structured eBird checklists with effort metadata. The present bird substrate and support-background construction differ, and the paper does not validate donor richness as an effort proxy.
evidence.suggested_location: Introduction or Discussion where community-science observation processes and recording richness are qualified.

csl.title: Fine-Tuning Can Distort Pretrained Features and Underperform Out-of-Distribution

evidence.supported_claim: Across ten computer-vision distribution-shift benchmarks, full fine-tuning improved average in-distribution accuracy but underperformed linear probing out of distribution; the authors also analyse this trade-off in a simplified theoretical setting.
evidence.relevance: Provides a non-ecological precedent for treating fine-tuning and frozen-feature transfer as distinct hypotheses under distribution shift.
evidence.limits: The data, losses, architectures and shifts are image-classification settings. It cannot explain the present ecological result, predict its sign or validate frozen-trunk superiority here, which was not observed on average.
evidence.suggested_location: At most one carefully qualified Discussion sentence; omit if the manuscript remains ecology-focused.

evidence.supported_claim: The review advocates analysing multiple bioclimatic models as ensembles to represent model-dependent uncertainty and describes bounding, consensus and probabilistic approaches.
evidence.relevance: Provides historical context for combining predictions and for treating ensemble performance as a question about complementary errors rather than a pretraining test.
evidence.limits: Its ensemble concept spans model classes, parameters, initial and boundary conditions and future scenarios; it does not validate a fixed equal-weight average of two fitted learners or show that such an average isolates pretraining value.
evidence.suggested_location: Discussion around the exploratory neural-conventional average if a general ensemble reference is desired; Valavi et al. (2022) is more directly relevant to the empirical caution.
